column1: Reconstruct Nietzsche's argument that God is dead and nihilism follows: premises, conclusion, the standard objection, and the reply.
column2: 1. Christian truthfulness itself — its own morality of honesty — finally turns against the Christian interpretation and finds it a lie (GM III). 2. So the Christian God becomes unbelievable to educated Europe: not refuted but abandoned (GS 125, 343). 3. Every value and authority was built on that belief, so its collapse devalues the whole table: the highest values devalue themselves. 4. Therefore Europe faces nihilism — existence without goal or answer to 'why?' — as a fate to be overcome, not a resting place. Objection: Secular values can simply be re-grounded. Reply: They remain Christian values on credit; ungrounded inheritance is precisely the nihilism he names.

column1: Reconstruct Nietzsche's perspectivism argument (GM III, section 12): premises, conclusion, the relativism objection, and the reply.
column2: 1. There is no 'immaculate perception': knowing is always done by a creature with drives, affects, and interests. 2. A perspective is therefore not an obstacle to knowledge but its condition. 3. 'Objectivity' cannot mean eliminating perspectives; it means command over them — employing a variety of perspectives in the service of knowledge. 4. Therefore the more eyes, different eyes, we bring to bear on a thing, the more complete our concept of it (GM III, section 12). Objection: Then every interpretation is as good as every other. Reply: No: perspectives rank by scope, honesty, and how much of the object they can hold.

column1: Explain genealogy as Nietzsche's method: what question it asks instead of 'is it true?', its tools, and its limit.
column2: Genealogy asks of a value not 'is it true?' but 'where did it come from, whom does it serve, and what is it worth for life?' Its tools are suspicious history, etymology, physiology, and psychology: ideals treated as symptoms of the type that needed them. The Genealogy's Preface and essays are the model, but the method is older — Human, All Too Human's 'history of moral feelings' is genealogy before the name. Its limit, conceded by defenders and pressed by critics: an origin story alone does not settle worth (the genetic fallacy). Genealogy destroys a value's aura and forces the question of its value; storytelling alone cannot answer it.

column1: Explain nihilism in Nietzsche's usage, including the passive/active distinction — and flag the source problem.
column2: Nihilism is the condition in which the highest values devalue themselves: the goal is lacking, the 'why?' finds no answer, existence appears meaningless. It is Nietzsche's diagnosis and a transition, never his position — he presents himself as the first complete nihilist of Europe precisely because he has lived nihilism through to overcome it. The familiar subdivision into passive nihilism (weary resignation; the last man's comfort) and active nihilism (strength clearing ground for new values) is drawn largely from the notebooks. Flag: that taxonomy is Nachlass material, systematized by editors and interpreters; the published works supply the diagnosis without the tidy labels.

column1: Explain decadence in Nietzsche's usage: the physiological meaning, its symptoms in philosophy and religion, and one application.
column2: Decadence is a physiological condition before it is a judgment: a state in which the instincts have grown anarchic, organization fails, and life chooses what harms it — prefers the means against its own flourishing. Its signature is needing stimulants against a fundamental exhaustion, and moralizing that exhaustion as virtue. Philosophy's decadent is Socrates: rationality at any price, dialectics as the weapon of a culture already declining. Religion's is the priest, who treats the sick herd by making it sicker — guilty. The concept is a diagnostic tool, not an insult: Nietzsche applies it to Wagner, to Christianity, and, in Ecce Homo, interrogates himself with it.

column1: Explain the Apollonian in The Birth of Tragedy: the drive, its art-form, and its limit.
column2: Apollo names a drive, not only a god: the drive to form, image, dream, and measure — the principium individuationis made beautiful. The Apollonian artist (Homer, Raphael, the sculptor) delights in appearance as appearance, holding the terror of existence at bay behind a shining, ordered dream. Its limit is built in: individuation is a veil. A culture of pure Apollo gets beautiful illusion and, in Socratic optimism, the demand that existence be intelligible — and loses the truth tragedy existed to bear. In the early system the Apollonian is therefore necessary and insufficient: it needs the Dionysian ground it conceals.

column1: Explain the Dionysian in The Birth of Tragedy: the drive, its art-form, and why music belongs to it.
column2: Dionysus names the counter-drive to Apollo: intoxication, the dissolution of the individual, the felt collapse of the principium individuationis into a primal unity of suffering and joy. Its art-form is music — because music, as the young Nietzsche takes over from Schopenhauer, speaks the underlying unity directly rather than copying appearances — and, supremely, Attic tragedy, where Dionysian truth is borne inside Apollonian form. The Dionysian is not mere chaos or release: it is knowledge — existence is terrible and absurd — experienced as ecstatic affirmation rather than denied. In the 1886 Self-Criticism Nietzsche keeps this affirmation and drops the Schopenhauerian metaphysics that first carried it.

column1: Explain master morality as a concept: its value-pair, its direction of evaluation, and its exemplar.
column2: Master morality is a mode of valuation before it is a code: the noble type experiences itself as value-creating, and its pair is good/bad — 'good' said first, spontaneously, of itself and its peers (powerful, proud, truthful, overflowing), 'bad' added afterward, almost as an afterthought, for the low, common, and timid. Evaluation runs from self-affirmation outward; no enemy is needed and none is hated — contempt replaces hatred. Its exemplars are the archaic aristocracies Nietzsche reads in Homer and the Roman nobility. It is a typology of value-creation, not Hegel's lordship dialectic and not a political program: masters in this sense are defined by how their values are born.

column1: Explain slave morality as a concept: its value-pair, its direction of evaluation, and what it needs to exist.
column2: Slave morality is the inverted mode of valuation: its pair is good/evil, and evaluation runs from negation inward. It begins by saying No to an external, hostile world — the master, the powerful, the 'evil one' — and only then, reactively, calls its own traits good: humility, patience, pity, and the weakness it cannot help, redescribed as merit. Where master morality creates from abundance, slave morality creates from ressentiment and needs an opposing world to define itself against. 'Slave' names a type and a psychology, not a census class: priests are its great artists, and herd morality is its modern, victorious form.

column1: Explain the free spirit: what it means in 1878, and how the figure develops by Beyond Good and Evil.
column2: In Human, All Too Human (1878) the free spirit is the emancipated thinker who has unlearned reverence: he tests inherited values against history, physiology, and the chemistry of concepts, accepting small, unapparent truths over metaphysical comforts. The figure is at first an Enlightenment type — Voltaire is its patron, and the 1878 dedication to him was a declaration of independence from Bayreuth. Across Daybreak and The Gay Science the free spirit gains gaiety and becomes an experimenter with himself. By Beyond Good and Evil the type is promoted: herald of the 'philosophers of the future,' no longer only a critic of old values but a legislator of new ones.

column1: Explain herd morality: its goods, its ruling passion, and its end-product.
column2: Herd morality is slave morality become the modern European norm: the valuation of the flock, whose goods are security, comfort, equality of condition, and the abolition of suffering and danger. Its ruling passion is pity joined to fear — whatever elevates an individual above the herd and intimidates the neighbor is called evil (Beyond Good and Evil, Part Five). The herd does not experience itself as a party with an interpretation; it experiences its values as morality itself, which is its strength and Nietzsche's target. Its end-product, in Zarathustra's Prologue, is the last man: riskless contentment that invented happiness and blinks.

column1: Explain sublimation in Nietzsche's psychology: the mechanism, and two places it does philosophical work.
column2: Sublimation is the redirection of a drive into a higher, culturally valuable form without extirpation: the drive is not denied or uprooted — the ascetic's method — but mastered, spiritualized, and given a new object. Cruelty sublimated becomes the intellectual conscience that turns suspicion on oneself; sexuality sublimated becomes art and knowledge as forms of love. Health, on this psychology, is not fewer drives but drives in rank order under a ruling taste. It also underwrites his reading of the philosopher: philosophy as the sublimated confession of its author's drives (Beyond Good and Evil, section 6).

column1: Explain Nietzsche's drive psychology (Triebe): the model of the self it replaces, and its consequence for moral judgment.
column2: The published works from Human, All Too Human onward replace the unitary soul with a polity: the self is a commonwealth of drives — inherited, competing, unequally strong — each with its own perspective and its will to discharge itself. Consciousness and reason are late, surface instruments of this economy, not its sovereign; 'a thought comes when it wishes, not when I wish.' Moral judgment is therefore re-described as symptomatology: a valuation expresses which drives rule in the type doing the valuing. This psychology is the engine under genealogy, the typology of morals, and will to power as self-overcoming.

column1: Reconstruct the master/slave typology argument (GM I; BGE section 260): premises, conclusion, the standard objection, and the reply.
column2: 1. Valuation has two directions: affirm oneself first and derive the negative term afterward, or negate an opponent first and derive oneself from the negation. 2. Archaic noble valuation runs the first way: good/bad, self-glorification before contempt. 3. Priestly-slave valuation runs the second: good/evil, the master's strength renamed evil so impotence can be renamed good. 4. Modern morality is the second type, victorious and invisible as a type — it presents itself as morality as such. Therefore our morality is one party's creation. Objection: The history is speculative ethnography. Reply: The typology is a diagnostic instrument: test it by the direction of evaluation in any morality you meet.

column1: Reconstruct the ressentiment argument (GM I, sections 10-11): premises, conclusion, the standard objection, and the reply.
column2: 1. Ressentiment is the reactive affect of those who cannot act: denied the deed, they take an imaginary revenge. 2. In the noble, resentment discharges at once; in the powerless it festers into a stance toward the world. 3. Held long enough, it becomes creative: it invents the 'evil one' and, against him, the 'good' man — itself. Therefore slave morality's values are born of ressentiment: its No is its creative deed, its love its hatred in disguise (GM I, sections 10-11). Objection: This psychologizes opponents instead of refuting them. Reply: That is the method's point — values are symptoms; the genealogy stands or falls as history and psychology.

column1: Reconstruct the slave revolt / priestly inversion argument (GM I, sections 7-8, 16): premises, conclusion, the standard objection, and the reply — flagged as his argument.
column2: 1. The priestly caste, bodily powerless but spiritually inventive, is the natural artist of ressentiment. 2. On Nietzsche's telling, priestly Judaism first performed the inversion: the noble equation good = powerful = beautiful = happy = beloved of God was reversed — the wretched alone are good, the powerful evil and damned. 3. Christianity universalized the revolt: with the cross, Rome was conquered by the values of the conquered. Therefore Europe's conscience-morality is the triumph of a priestly act of revenge. Objection: The history is tendentious, the psychology unfalsifiable. Reply: Defenders rest the case on the typology and the values' logic. This is his argument — not established history.

column1: Reconstruct the bad conscience argument (GM II, sections 16-22): premises, conclusion, the standard objection, and the reply.
column2: 1. Man's instincts of cruelty, domination, and change were once discharged outward. 2. Enclosure within society and the state blocked that discharge; instincts that cannot leave turn inward — this internalization is the origin of the soul's depth. 3. Denied their object, the instincts take the self as object: man judges and punishes himself — bad conscience, a sickness, but pregnant. 4. The priest and the Christian God then maximize it: debt (Schuld) before God becomes guilt that can never be discharged (GM II, sections 16-22). Therefore guilt is historical: cruelty institutionalized, then theologized. Objection: Conjectural natural history. Reply: A genealogical hypothesis, judged by what it explains about guilt.

column1: Reconstruct the sovereign individual argument (GM II, sections 1-3): premises, conclusion, the standard objection, and the reply.
column2: 1. Breeding an animal permitted to promise required a memory of the will: millennia of custom, enforced by pain, made man calculable. 2. Its ripest fruit is the sovereign individual: master of a free will in the only sense Nietzsche honors — not metaphysical liberty but earned self-command (GM II, sections 1-3). 3. He is the genealogy's internal counter-ideal: conscience turned affirmative, promising as strength rather than guilt as sickness. Therefore the history of conscience has a second outcome: autonomy. Objection: An aristocratic exception abandoning everyone else to the herd. Reply: Nietzsche accepts the terms: a late, rare fruit, offered as a direction, not a policy.

column1: Reconstruct the ascetic ideal argument (GM III): premises, conclusion, the standard objection, and the reply.
column2: 1. Suffering is not the problem; meaningless suffering is — man curses the senselessness, not the pain. 2. The ascetic ideal supplied a meaning: suffering as guilt and purification, administered by the priest, who organized the herd and saved it from nihilism. 3. The meaning is a will turned against life — man would rather will nothingness than not will — whose latest form is science, its will to truth the ideal's own kernel (GM III 24-28). Therefore the ideal is humanity's preservation device and its sickness in one. Objection: One 'ideal' flattens real differences. Reply: The claim concerns a shared valuation — life justified only by being denied.

column1: Reconstruct the 'no doer behind the deed' argument (BGE section 17; GM I, section 13): premises, conclusion, the standard objection, and the reply.
column2: 1. Grammar posits a subject for every activity: lightning and its flash, strength and its expression — a doer added to the deed. 2. The doubling is grammar's seduction, not a discovery: no neutral substratum stands behind the doing. 3. Slave morality needs the fiction: only if the strong man is a free subject behind his strength can he be blamed for exercising it — and the lamb call its weakness chosen virtue (BGE 17; GM I.13). Therefore morality's free, responsible subject is a grammatical artifact. Objection: Without a doer, responsibility collapses. Reply: That collapse is the destination for morality's version; rank and necessity survive it.

column1: Reconstruct the will to power argument in its published form (BGE section 36): premises, conclusion, the status dispute, and the objection.
column2: 1. Suppose — the section's own form — nothing is given as real except our desires and passions. 2. Suppose further that all organic functions trace back to one form of will: drives seeking discharge, growth, and the overcoming of resistance. 3. Then one may define all efficient force univocally as will to power: the world viewed from inside, will to power and nothing besides. Therefore will to power stands as an interpretive hypothesis of maximal scope. Status dispute: psychology only, full metaphysics, or heuristic lens — unresolved. Objection: The section supposes what it claims to discover. The Nachlass 'book' of this title is his sister's construction.

column1: Explain pathos of distance (BGE section 257): the feeling, what it produces, and why Nietzsche calls it the origin of 'good'.
column2: Pathos of distance is the ingrained feeling of an order of rank between types — distance experienced within the soul itself, and wanting it wider. In Beyond Good and Evil section 257 Nietzsche credits it with producing, in aristocratic ages, the tension from which higher culture grows: the craving for ever wider distance that raises the type man. He goes further: the origin of the antithesis good/bad itself lies in this pathos — the noble's felt distance from the low is the first valuation. Distance is therefore not snobbery but a generative condition: where rank is leveled as shameful, the conditions of enhancement are dismantled.

column1: Explain revaluation (Umwertung) as Nietzsche's project-name: what is revalued, by what standard, and where the project is stated.
column2: Revaluation of all values is the name of Nietzsche's whole late project (the subtitle of The Antichrist; the planned main work's title — a plan, not a delivered book). What is revalued is the inherited table itself: pity, humility, equality, selflessness — slave morality's goods — re-estimated by a standard they cannot supply. The standard is life: does a value serve ascending, self-overcoming life, or declining, self-preserving life? The project is executed piecemeal — the Genealogy's demand for a critique of moral values, Twilight's hammer-sounding of idols, Ecce Homo's retrospect — never as a finished new table, which is why interpreters dispute its content.

column1: Reconstruct eternal recurrence as a test (GS section 341): the thought experiment, what decides the response, and the cosmology dispute — flagged.
column2: 1. A demon proposes: this life, exactly as lived, will recur eternally — every pain and joy in the same sequence, nothing new. 2. The proposal is either crushing — you curse the demon — or it becomes the greatest weight: you answer that you have never heard anything more divine. 3. What decides is not evidence but whether you can will your life again without editing out its suffering (GS section 341). Therefore, on the standard reading, recurrence is a selective test of affirmation. Dispute: Notebook sketches argue a literal cosmology; they are Nachlass, and the test reading rests on the published text.

column1: Explain amor fati: the formula, its first statement, and how it differs from resignation or optimism.
column2: Amor fati — love of one's fate — is Nietzsche's formula for greatness: to want nothing to be different, not forward, not backward, not in all eternity; not merely to bear what is necessary, still less to conceal it, but to love it. First stated as a New Year's resolution at The Gay Science section 276 (1882) and canonized in Ecce Homo, it is neither resignation (enduring necessity while wishing otherwise) nor optimism (editing the record and calling the edit hope). It is an affirmative discipline toward one's whole past: the stance recurrence tests, and the opposite of revenge against time and its 'it was.'

column1: Explain the Ubermensch: what the figure is, what it is not, and its textual situation.
column2: Zarathustra's Ubermensch (overman) is the figure who creates values after the death of God and remains faithful to the meaning of the earth rather than inventing heavens to devalue it. He is an aspiration and a direction — man as a rope between animal and overman — not an existing type, a biological master race, or a political program; Nietzsche's contempt for anti-Semitism and German nationalism is on the published page. Textual caution: the figure belongs to Thus Spoke Zarathustra, his most literary and least argumentative book, and barely appears elsewhere in the published works; readings that build the whole philosophy on it outrun the evidence.

column1: Explain the last man: the portrait, where it appears, and the work it does against herd morality.
column2: The last man is Zarathustra's counter-figure to the Ubermensch, drawn in the Prologue: the most contemptible man, who makes everything small — no shepherd and one herd, everyone wanting the same, work as entertainment, a little poison now and then for pleasant dreams, and 'we have invented happiness,' say the last men, and they blink. He is not the ressentiment slave of the Genealogy but something later and quieter: the end-product of herd morality perfected, comfort without longing, in which even contempt has gone slack. His work in the argument is diagnostic: against the last man, nihilism is not dramatic despair but contentment — the danger modernity actually faces.

column1: Explain the three metamorphoses (Zarathustra, Part One): camel, lion, child — what each can and cannot do.
column2: Self-overcoming is the form will to power takes when its nearest resistance is the self. Life, Zarathustra is told, is that which must always overcome itself: every drive's discharge meets the counter-pressure of the other drives, and health is the hierarchy achieved by that inner war, not its absence. The doctrine disciplines the crude reading of will to power as domination of others — the primary scene of command and obedience is within a soul and a culture, and the highest types (the sovereign individual, the philosopher-legislator) are products of long self-constraint. Anchors: Zarathustra, 'On Self-Overcoming'; Beyond Good and Evil section 259.

column1: Explain self-overcoming (Selbstuberwindung): its place in the will to power doctrine, and one textual anchor.
column2: Self-overcoming is the form will to power takes when its nearest resistance is the self. Life, Zarathustra is told, is that which must always overcome itself: every drive's discharge meets the counter-pressure of the other drives, and health is the hierarchy achieved by that inner war, not its absence. The doctrine disciplines the crude reading of will to power as domination of others — the primary scene of command and obedience is within a soul and a culture, and the highest types (the sovereign individual, the philosopher-legislator) are products of long self-constraint. Anchors: Zarathustra, 'On Self-Overcoming'; Beyond Good and Evil section 259.

column1: Explain the pessimism of strength (GS section 370; the 1886 Self-Criticism): the two pessimisms, and Nietzsche's verdict on Schopenhauer's.
column2: Nietzsche distinguishes two pessimisms by the pessimist's condition. Romantic pessimism — Schopenhauer's, Wagner's — is the pessimism of weakness: suffering from the impoverishment of life, it longs for rest, redemption, denial of the will; a symptom of decline calling itself wisdom. Against it stands a pessimism of strength, later Dionysian pessimism: suffering from the overfullness of life, it faces existence's terrible character without flinching and affirms it, needing no rescue. The Birth of Tragedy is retrospectively claimed for the second kind (GS section 370; the 1886 Self-Criticism). The distinction is the hinge of the Schopenhauer inheritance: same diagnosis of suffering, opposite physiology, opposite prescription.

column1: Explain Schuld: the debt/guilt complex at the root of Nietzsche's account of conscience (GM II).
column2: Schuld is the German word meaning both debt and guilt, and Genealogy II builds the conscience out of that double sense. In the creditor–debtor relation — among the oldest human relations — the debtor who cannot repay pledges himself: his body, his freedom, his pain become payable equivalents, and cruelty toward the defaulter is the creditor's compensation. Memory and the power to promise are bred into humans so contracts can hold. Turned religious, debt becomes guilt before ancestors, then gods, and finally the Christian God, where it is declared unpayable: maximal debt as maximal guilt. Conscience, on this account, began as bookkeeping, not as a moral voice.

column1: Reconstruct the Schopenhauer inversion: the shared premises, the single refused premise, and Nietzsche's counter-prescription.
column2: Shared: (1) existence is striving — Schopenhauer's Will; Nietzsche's drives and will to power; (2) willing springs from lack, so suffering is structural: satisfaction is brief, boredom and new desire follow; (3) intellect is striving's instrument, not its master. Refused: (4) Schopenhauer's valuation — that this structure indicts existence and licenses denial of the will, with compassion as ethics and resignation as wisdom. Nietzsche inverts the prescription, keeping the diagnosis: suffering's structural place is the condition of growth, so the answer is affirmation — amor fati, recurrence willed, values created — and Schopenhauerian pity is unmasked as the will to nothingness in moral dress (GS 370; GM, Preface).

column1: Explain the great health (GS section 382): the concept, and why it closes the expanded Gay Science.
column2: The great health is the health of a free spirit who has been sick and recovered repeatedly — a health 'that one does not merely have but acquires continually, and must acquire because one gives it up again and again.' It names robustness as a practice: taking poisons as stimulants, making every experience — including nihilism lived through — material for growth, setting out for an undiscovered land of health. Section 382 closes Book V of The Gay Science (1887) and points toward Zarathustra's creator: the great health is the physiological name of the figure who can will new values. Compare decadence — the same economy, failing.

column1: Explain the ascetic priest as a type (GM III): his function for the herd, his method, and his paradox.
column2: The ascetic priest is the Third Essay's antagonist and, in Nietzsche's typology, history's most powerful human type: shepherd of the suffering herd. His function is to give suffering a meaning — he redirects ressentiment inward ('you alone are to blame for your suffering'), organizes the sick into a flock, and combats their depression with mechanical activity, petty pleasures, love of neighbor, and orgies of feeling. The paradox is structural, not hypocrisy: he is himself the will turned against life, a decadent who must make his patients sicker — guilty — to rule them, yet he preserves them, saving the will itself from suicidal nihilism.
